title: Driving Business with Tech: A Conversation with a Customer Engineer

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Hello guys, and welcome to another episode of TechPeeps Diaspora. As usual on this show, we bring you stories of successful tech Africans, um, living around the world. And today we have yet another story for you. Um, probably something less technical than we usually have on the show. Um, yeah, help me welcome my guest, Isaac. Hi Isaac, welcome to the show.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Hey, how's it going?

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Yeah, I'm doing pretty well. Um, so like, how is the winter in, um, US or what part of the US actually?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Yeah, so I'm based in Atlanta, Georgia. Um, and we typically don't have as much snow or cold. Uh, but over the past, I'll say 2 weeks, it has been very cold, but thankfully things have warmed up a little, so I think it's been very nice. At, at, at this point in time.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Yeah. Like at least I'm happy it's not as, you know, bad as Berlin. Not that it's like the winter this year has been very favorable, I'd say.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: So nice.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Yeah. Um, so Isaac is a customer success engineer. That's right. Um, at Google. Um, and yeah, I'm not gonna take that away. So Isaac, could you, um, give a brief introduction about yourself? Sounds good.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Um, so my name is Isaac. I am originally from Accra, Ghana, and I currently work as a customer engineer at Google Cloud. Google Cloud is Google's cloud division within the company. I moved to the US in 2018, so I was actually, um, an international student at the University of Miami. So I went to college, I did high school and I did college in Ghana But I did college for only a year and eventually moved here. And in school, I majored in computer science and minored in math. And throughout my time in college, I got to try a variety of different things. One of the things I tried was being a tutor. So I tutored all my 4 years of college. I also was involved in a variety of different clubs and initiatives, some very technical, including Sturdy and Developer Student Club. Within Miami's campus sponsored by Google, as well as interning with a telecommunications API company called Twilio. So eventually all those experiences led me to an interview opportunity in August of 2021 with Google, and I eventually got a role called the Cloud Technical Residency role, which was a 9-month residency program That eventually placed me, um, as a customer engineer after the, the training. So I've been doing, I've been at Google for about 2 and a half years and I've been a customer engineer for a year and a half. And, and yeah, that's been my journey so far. So.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Yeah, sounds amazing. Um, I guess the natural question for me is what is a customer success engineer?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Sounds good. So I always use this analogy as a customer engineer is a technical liaison within a given engagement. Um, and typically, typically those engagements are sales engagements. So, um, in the cloud business in particular, you have different companies or individuals or startups that want to essentially buy services on the cloud. When people think about the cloud, they usually think about storage and storing devices, but the cloud comprises of a variety of different things. So it can include storage, data analytics, it can include compute, different services that companies will benefit from. So essentially the cloud business allows you to purchase a unit of that computation for your particular purpose. So usually you need sellers to actually sell a lot of these services. Um, but within those sales engagements, you always need someone technical to translate a lot of the, the technical jargon in between both parties, whether it's the seller's party or the buyer's party. Um, so a customer engineer essentially is that technical liaison who, um, does that translation and also helps enable that account where it is to make that purchasing decision. Um, so for example, if a startup wants to build, um, a service on the cloud essentially for data analytics. Let's, let's pick that for example. What a customer engineer would do within those sales engagements is they would have that initial discovery call to see what does this customer want to build, uh, what is this customer, or what does this customer see itself in the next 2 months, um, 6 months, a year. And we actually can help capacity plan for those changes. So Um, essentially you are like a technical guide, a guardian, a consultant, but you don't necessarily implement everything, but you provide that guidance, um, for the customer to move forward. So yeah, that's kind of like the, the details of how the role works.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Um, so I'm guessing the reason why, like, it's important, like this role has, like, sounds like it has a bridge between like technical and also having some sales experience and probably the reason why the technical bit is Um, important is, yeah, most likely interacting with, you know, like their customers are mostly like also technical people, like probably, um, software engineers, I'm guessing, or like, um, you know, data engineers, um, people who are technical. And therefore it's easier maybe for the salespeople, for someone who speaks the same language, right? To, to understand what Um, they need. Sounds like a really interesting role.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Yeah. Um, the cool thing, and you raised that in the earlier question, is that we talk to a variety of different people. Um, I will say the vast majority are technical, but sometimes you do have different personas. So you, okay, could be talking, um, on one call to a CEO and the next call is a data scientist. So that's basically where you have to kind of like navigate between the two cuz Depending on the person you're talking to, it would, it'll kind of like change the way you are even like talking about a particular technology and how you are value selling. That's the, the best way to describe it because at the end of the day, you are influencing a purchasing decision.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Um, there are companies that want to spend money to build a particular service. So technical jargon can only go so far.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Um, you want to kind of like phrase things and explain things in such a way that they know what they're getting into and can understand it within their own knowledge domains.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: So yeah. Yeah. I've seen like, uh, different roles spun up, um, like within sometimes, you know, within different organizations, like, uh, for instance, developer advocates, also developer relations. Like, I'm curious, how does this differ to like a customer success engineer?

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Yeah. So, um, Again, from the name, like customer engineer, customer success engineer, or solutions engineer, every company has the way it, it, it words that.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Um, those roles are mainly focused on one-to-one customer, um, engagements. That's kind of like one-to-one. Sometimes we do one-to-many stuff where we go to events and we give talks. So that, that typically is the case. But a developer advocate is more focused or it's more community focused. So that's kind of like the emphasis there where, um, there's a particular technology or a particular stack or particular methodology that they want to educate, uh, or advocate for within the community. Uh, so when I work at Twilio, that's one of the biggest things we would do. Um, there was always like a huge emphasis on education and educating developers on a particular API.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Um, so that's where a developer advocate is because essentially what their role is, is they're evangelizing that particular tool. And so they make videos, they might actually do one-to-one events, but the emphasis is more or less focused on community engagement. Mm-hmm. Whereas a customer engineer is more directly one-to-one because our incentives are kind of like to drive those individual, um, businesses. Uh, and Advocate is more focused on the wider audience and the wider community building. So.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Yeah. Interesting. So you mentioned earlier that, you know, you don't really get to implement some of these, you know, solutions. Yeah. Like what's the balance between technical and sales? If—

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: That's a really good question. And I feel like in my domain I've met 2 different strands. So I think for a role like this, you definitely need to be technical. You need to have technical know-how of how the, a lot of the underlying technologies work, because you can only speak to something you've tried or know how it works, cuz you are speaking to audiences who need a lot of these things implemented. Uh, so that's the first thing. Um, I do think there are customer engineers who are more sales-centric, so they can talk about solutions or talk about, um, maybe specific architectures that are more like salesy. Uh, by the end of the day, every customer is also very different, right? And every customer is coming to you for something. So the sales skills or the technical skills can only go so far individually.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Um, so what I've seen has helped for me is just doing that initial discovery. What does this customer want? Why are they here? Where do they want to go? And trying to come up with a solution that fits their needs. And that comes more or less with like experience as opposed to like I know so much about something technically, or I know so much about how to sell a product. Um, so it's a weird, um, combination of customer empathy where you care about the person's needs, Mm-hmm. but you are also kind of like taking a lot of the technical stuff you've learned, whether about a particular technology or a stack, and trying to mesh all these together, um, to influence again that sales decision. Or because again, A customer is dedicating their time, energy, and resources to use a particular service. So you want to make sure that they're well informed about what they're doing, but at the same time also earn your trust about that particular solution. So, um, I will say it's a little bit of both. Um, but the cool, the amazing thing about just being in customer engineering is that you get to grow across both fields because a good software developer is only as good if they can sell their product.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: And a good salesperson is only as good if their products are good. So it's kind of like the best of both worlds in my role.

segments.text: Yeah, I can give a brief glimpse into it. So a lot of my day is typically, um, set managing like a book of business. CRM is a content management tool, and essentially like Salesforce or any tool they have a list of accounts that they need to kind of like, quote unquote, manage.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Um, and the way we businesses will track this management is through specific quarterly metrics. Um, so my typical day would be analyzing a lot of those metrics to see how those accounts are doing in terms of spend. A typical activity within that day would be customer calls. So usually I have like 30-minute calls spread across my day where we go onto calls, whether intro calls, learning about what a customer is doing and what they want to implement, or deep dive tech discovery calls. So for example, there are times where I hop onto a call and a customer wants to do an architecture review. They've designed a system, let's say a database system or like an AI system. that he wants my opinion on, and we can get to explain that to them and explain the products within Google Cloud or any cloud that fits that particular mode. So that's one part of my day. A lot of those video calls will transcend to like follow-up emails or follow-up messages on Slack or Google Chat. We also do a lot of one-to-many enablements. I think you asked the question about developer advocacy.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: So that's one key part of being a customer engineer is that you also want to create content that other customer engineers can use and other people in the community can use. So we do a, a lot of events. So occasionally I have to plan a lot of outreach stuff either via email or via LinkedIn where I talk about particular technology. I cite customer examples and testimonials. Um, just mainly educating customers on everything. So. I would say about 60% of my day is a lot of the customer engagement, whether it's emails, video calls, actual calls. That's very rare, but sometimes those happen. I'll say another 20% is preparing for a lot of those big-scale events. We typically do them once a month. My company sometimes once a quarter. And I'll say the last 20% is also enablement. I need to make sure that I'm ramping up with a lot of the technology that's going on. So I know particularly in the realm of AI, things are changing every week or every day. So I have to make sure I'm educated and I can apply this to my engagement. So that's how, uh, things are.

segments.text: Yeah. Um, um, you know, curious to see if, you know, I don't know if you're free to talk about like the compensation structure for like, uh, some of these roles. Um, you know, what your CV should look like, uh, what kind of past experiences you can lean on, for example.

segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: HOST

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: Yeah, so I can talk about my experience. Um, I don't think it's applicable for everyone, but it might be very similar. So when I interned with Twilio my junior year— my junior year was my third year in the US— um, I, I ended up finishing the internship, and at the very end of it, I got approached by a recruiter on LinkedIn, and it was for a particular role at Google called the Cloud Technical Residency. So essentially this role was designed to train people to become technical sellers because a lot of people leaving college again have a lot of the technical knowledge but they don't have a lot of business savvy, sales rapport. So, um, I did the interview. I did like 4 rounds of different things we're testing for. So it was a very technical, um, from questions around how does the internet work, stuff like that, protocols, how to architect a solution, to very, very sales-specific questions, including coding as well.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: GUEST
segments.text: So typically for roles like this, I will say you want to kind of frame your experiences around how you've enabled customers and what impact you've had. So that's kind of like how you would stand out in that pool of like roles. I'll also say I also work as a tutor, and I also work in a lot of roles that involve community building and community enablement. And so those are things to point out and highlight because again, the technology stack and everything is good, but you also want to be able to highlight how that impacts a community and how many people you've been able to influence. So that's another thing. And the last thing is also just make sure that your experiences align with a lot of the requirements. Because again, it could be a customer engineer role, solution engineer role, but it might require 5 years of experience. And you might not have that 5 years of experience. So that's another thing to point out. And the last thing is also having relevant projects.

segments.speaker: HOST
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.text: Mm-hmm.
